verdicts.note: Facts verified in the docs and the Go source. The server generates the key pair, seals it in PostgreSQL with the master key and signs every manifest itself, so anyone who can publish gets their update signed. The master key cannot be recovered. IP allowlists and SSO are Enterprise features. The certificate the server generates is valid for 10 years, which is long enough. The high severity stands. The recommendation does not.
verdicts.correction: 'Generate the key with eoas generate-certs and hand it to xprem at first boot' is not a documented option on a fresh control-plane install. Local or environment keys are sealed in only during the one-time v2 to v3 import. The workable offline backup is the master key itself, plus the xprem database inside the existing PostgreSQL backups; with both, the signing key can be restored. The dashboard (USE_DASHBOARD=true) is served by the same process as the public manifest endpoint. verdicts.note: The finding is right that the plan needs an explicit runtimeVersion rule, and xprem's warning against fingerprint is verified. Its chosen rule is unsafe for this plan.
verdicts.correction: If a fixed runtimeVersion is bumped only when native code changes, two store versions can share one runtime. A conformant server then sends the newest update for that runtime to both, so a fix published from a newer release brings that release's new features to older binaries. That breaks plan line 507 ('yeni özellik yeni sürümle gelir') and DPLA 3.3.1(C). Use the appVersion policy: the runtime equals the app version and changes at every public APK or App Store release. Publish each fix from that release's branch, and keep the number of live versions small with the minimum-version check. Still avoid fingerprint.

recommendation_issues.problem: The fixed code for the demo instructor is a standing credential. Keep it only in App Store Connect and the server's secret settings, never in the repo. 'Bireysel hesabımla başvururum' rests only on the unlisted page and ignores guideline 5.1.1(ix), which App Review used in May 2026 to require an organization account for a private app handling user data. The part about the İÜ account and the fee waiver is unverified for Türkiye (the waiver page lists only example authorities) and edges into the owner's excluded 'sponsors' topic. The S3-compatible bucket adds an external account and credentials. The only technical reason xprem gives against local disk is running several instances, and the plan runs one Compose container. Local disk on a backed-up volume is the compact choice unless xprem is scaled out or the server cannot handle the download traffic. If a bucket is used, it should be the hosting provider's managed storage, not a self-hosted S3 server. Also, 'sunucu değişse de yeniden derleme gerekmez' holds only if the signing key moves with it (master key plus xprem database). With the database key store, xprem documents no way to export the private key to a different server implementation.

'İmza anahtarını kendim üretirim ve xprem'e ilk açılışta öyle veririm' is not a documented control-plane path. Keys come from the database store or AWS Secrets Manager only, and xprem says file paths and environment variables are not offered. Adding AWS Secrets Manager only for this would be bloat. Back up the master key offline and include the xprem database in the existing PostgreSQL backups instead. 'Panel yalnız SSH tüneliyle açılır' also needs a reverse-proxy rule for /dashboard, because the dashboard runs in the same process as the public manifest endpoint. The simpler option is to leave USE_DASHBOARD off except during admin sessions.

A fixed runtimeVersion bumped only on native changes lets two store versions share a runtime. The server then sends the newest update for that runtime to both, so a fix built from a newer release carries that release's new features to older binaries. This conflicts with plan line 507 and DPLA 3.3.1(C). Use the appVersion policy (the runtime changes at every public release).

The simplification stands, but the reason is narrower than stated. GitHub needs a token only if one is used. A server-side read of the latest release with a cache needs a few requests per hour, far under the unauthenticated limit of 60 per hour, unless the server shares its public IP. The CI-written file, in turn, needs a credentialed path from CI to the server. Either single source is fine.

verdict_reason: No high-severity finding was refuted or left unverifiable. S12-F5, the only high item, holds on its facts (checked in the docs and the Go source). It is CORRECTED only in its recommendation: a fresh control-plane install documents no way to bring your own key except AWS Secrets Manager, so the backup should be the master key plus the xprem database. Two other findings were corrected. S12-F3: guideline 5.1.1(ix) can require an organization account. S12-F6: runtimeVersion must change at every public release, otherwise OTA fixes carry new features to older binaries. The other 8 findings are confirmed. Two checked_ok items are disputed: the benchmark claim about asset serving holds only with object storage, and App Store phased release covers only automatic updates on iPhone. The researcher missed four items, all medium or low: the 5.1.1(ix) risk for an individual account, whether data survives the TestFlight to App Store switch, a named fallback for xprem, and update checks on every app launch. No high-severity miss remains, so the slice passes with these corrections applied.
